blocks.text: The financial reality of high turnover

When a property manager leaves, your business loses more than just a person. You lose operational intelligence that is hard to replace. This includes knowledge of building quirks, vendor relationships, and specific tenant needs. This knowledge evaporation directly impacts your bottom line.

Replacing an employee costs between 40 and 200 percent of their annual salary. This covers the cost of recruiting, training, and the dip in productivity while a new person learns the ropes. Maintenance resolution times often jump by 40 percent in the three months after a manager leaves. This causes tenant dissatisfaction and can lead to lease renewals dropping.
Why do property managers change so often

The primary reason is burnout. Property managers are expected to be available at all hours. They juggle demands from owners, tenants, and contractors. When you add manual data entry into the mix, the job becomes overwhelming.

items: Phone overload and after hours demands.
Repetitive manual tasks like rent reconciliation.
Lack of clear career growth paths.
Feeling underpaid for the complexity of the work.

blocks.text: Fixing the retention problem without extra costs
You do not need to buy expensive new software to start fixing your retention issues. You can change how your team works today. Focus on these three areas to make the daily grind more manageable.

Many managers spend hours on tasks that can be handled by simple automation. Use your existing property management platform to set up automated responses for common maintenance requests. If a tenant emails about a leaky faucet, the system should acknowledge the request and provide a timeline. This stops the manager from manually typing the same email ten times a day.

New hires often quit because they feel lost. Create a 90 day plan for every new employee. Pair them with a mentor who can answer questions about building operations. When a new manager knows exactly what is expected of them, they are more likely to stay.
Create a culture of frequent feedback

Stop waiting for annual reviews to tell someone they are doing a good job. A quick check in once a week can change everything. Publicly recognize small wins during your team meetings. This makes staff feel like their contribution is actually seen.
